name: CH455G
title: CH455: four-digit LED display driver and 28-key keyboard scanner with 2-wire serial interface
summary: The CH455 multiplexes four common-cathode seven-segment digits with decimal point, or 32 LEDs in an 8 by 4 matrix, and scans a 7 by 4 matrix of up to 28 keys, all on an internal oscillator. A host controls it over a two-wire SCL/SDA interface at up to 4 MHz that works with I²C buses, and reads keys either on an active-low interrupt or by polling. Segment outputs source at least 25 mA and digit outputs sink at least 160 mA, with eight duty-cycle brightness steps, a sleep mode woken by a key or a command, and power-on reset. CH455K (DIP18) and CH455H (SOP18) have INT# and ISET pins; CH455G (SOP16) has neither.
key_figures: 4 digits × 8 segments (8×4) or 7×4 in 7-segment mode; 32 LEDs
2.5 V min, 5 V typ, 5.3 V max; 2.7 V to 5 V supported

circuits.title: Four common-cathode digits and a 28-key matrix
circuits.description: An 8051 talks to a CH455K/H over SCL and SDA, with INT# wired to its INT0 input. The chip multiplexes four common-cathode digits: every digit's like segments are joined, and each SEG output reaches that bus through a 100 Ω resistor; ISET is grounded, so the internal current limit is off and the resistors set and balance segment current. Each digit's cathode returns to its DIG pin through a diode, which blocks reverse leakage of the display and raises the level the SEG inputs see during key scan. A 7 by 4 grid of push buttons sits between the segment bus rows SEG0 to SEG6 and four columns, each column fed from its DIG pin through 10 kΩ so a pressed key cannot short a SEG line to a DIG line. C1 and C2 decouple the supply at the chip.

circuits.title: Four common-anode digits with PNP digit drivers
circuits.description: A CH455G drives four common-anode digits. Each DIG output, which pulls low for its digit, turns on a 9012 PNP through 1 kΩ; the transistor's emitter is on VCC and its collector feeds that digit's common anode, so the transistor inverts the DIG signal. The SEG outputs sink segment current through 100 Ω resistors on the segment bus. C3 and C4 decouple the supply.

circuits.title: Four common-anode digits with P-MOSFET digit drivers
circuits.description: A CH455G drives four common-anode digits through four 2301 P-channel MOSFETs, one per digit: each DIG output drives a gate directly and the drain feeds that digit's common anode. The sources share a node one diode drop below VCC, set by a 1N4001; that drop, in place of segment resistors, holds down the total current. SEG outputs go straight to the segment bus. C3 and C4 decouple the supply.

circuits.title: Four seven-segment digits and seven keys on the SOP16 part
circuits.description: A low-cost layout for the CH455G, which has no INT# pin. The chip runs in 7-segment mode, so SEG7 becomes the active-low key interrupt and the decimal points are unused. SEG0 to SEG6 drive segments A to G of four common-cathode digits directly, relying on the internal current limit, and DIG0 to DIG3 drive the cathodes. Seven keys connect SEG0 to SEG6 to one column, which is fed from DIG0 through 4.7 kΩ. C6 and C5 decouple the supply.

circuits.title: Interface hardened against noise on long lines
circuits.description: A controller on one board reaches a CH455K/H on another over a cable carrying VCC, GND, SCL, SDA and INT#. At the chip end, 200 Ω series resistors R18 and R19 and 100 pF capacitors C11 and C12 to ground filter SDA and SCL; R8 and R9, 4.7 kΩ to VCC on the controller side of the series resistors, strengthen the pull-up of quasi-bidirectional port pins. C10, 100 pF at the controller, filters INT#. Each board decouples its own supply.

operation.text: Display drive and key scanning are independent functions that the host turns on, off and configures by command. The serial interface is implemented in hardware, so frequent fast host access does not slow the chip's own work. Binary values are written with a trailing B and hexadecimal with a trailing H.

Digits are scanned in turn from DIG0 to DIG3; only one DIG pin sinks current at a time. The built-in drivers handle common-cathode digits from 0.5 inch to 1 inch directly: SEG6 to SEG0 drive segments G to A, SEG7 the decimal point, and DIG3 to DIG0 the four cathodes. The outputs can instead drive an 8 by 4 LED matrix or 32 single LEDs, common-anode digits through external inverting drivers, or large digits through external power transistors. In 7-segment mode SEG7 carries the key interrupt and cannot drive a decimal point.

Each digit's scan slot is split into eight parts, and the duty setting lights from 1/8 to 8/8 of them. A higher duty gives more average current and a brighter display, though brightness does not follow duty linearly.
Four 8-bit registers hold one byte per digit (or per group of eight LEDs). Bits 7 to 0 map to DP and segments G to A; in an LED matrix every bit is one LED. A 1 lights the segment or LED.

Key scans are slotted into the display scan at intervals. During a scan DIG0 to DIG3 drive high one after another while the rest stay low, and SEG0 to SEG6 stop driving and act as inputs held low by internal pull-downs; a pressed key between, say, DIG1 and SEG4 shows SEG4 high while DIG1 is high. A key counts only if two successive scans agree, which rejects bounce and interference. A valid key's code is latched and INT# pulls low; no further interrupt is raised until a new valid key is found. SEG1 and SEG0 on the same DIG form a combination key that takes top priority; otherwise, among keys pressed together, the one with the lower code wins.

The key code may be read at any time, but is normally read after the interrupt, when bit 6 is always 1. To learn when the key is released, the host polls the code until bit 6 becomes 0. Example: the key between DIG1 and SEG4 reads 01100101B (65H) while pressed and usually 00100101B (25H) after release.

SCL is an input with pull-up and idles high; SDA is a quasi-bidirectional line with pull-up and idles high; INT# is an open-drain output with pull-up that idles high and serves as the key interrupt once key scanning is on. Data goes most significant bit first, high for 1. The chip samples SDA on the SCL rising edge and changes its SDA output on the SCL falling edge. SDA falling while SCL is high is a start; SDA rising while SCL is high is a stop. Commands are accepted only after a start, so SCL can be shared with other circuits as long as SDA is held still, and both lines can be shared if SDA only changes while SCL is low. After the interrupt, a read restores INT# high and returns the key code on SDA.

Every exchange is six steps: start, byte 1, acknowledge 1, byte 2, acknowledge 2, stop. In a write the host sends byte 2; in a read the chip sends it. Both acknowledges are fixed at 1. A write of 48H then 01H turns the display on in 8-segment mode at full duty.

Byte 1 is 48H; byte 2 carries KOFF, INTENS, 7SEG, SLEEP and ENA, and the display data is untouched. Examples of byte 2: 00000001B is 8-segment mode at 8/8 duty; 01000001B is 8-segment mode at 4/8; 00001001B is 7-segment mode at 8/8; 00000101B enters sleep. 7-segment mode, where SEG7 behaves like INT#, is mainly for the CH455G, which lacks an INT# pin.

Setting SLEEP puts the chip into low-power sleep. Either a key on SEG3 to SEG0 (valid codes 44H to 5FH) or the next command wakes it, and SLEEP clears itself. Sleep and wake leave all other state as it was. If ENA is 1, waking raises a key interrupt; if ENA is 0, it does not.
Byte 1 is the register address, 68H, 6AH, 6CH or 6EH for the digits on DIG0 to DIG3; byte 2 is the 8-bit digit data. Writing 6CH then 79H makes the digit on DIG2 show E.

Byte 1 is 4FH and byte 2 comes back from the chip: it is the only command that returns data. The host must release SDA (tri-state or pulled high) before the chip drives it. All eight bits are valid: bit 6 is the status and bits 5 to 0 the scan code.

ISET left open gives the default segment current. A resistor from ISET to VCC raises its voltage and reduces the segment current; a resistor to GND lowers its voltage and increases it. Tying ISET to GND turns the internal current limit off, after which series segment resistors set the current.

The SOP16 part has no INT# pin. To scan keys it either runs in 7-segment mode, giving up the decimal points and using SEG7 as the interrupt, or stays in 8-segment mode while the host polls the key code.

The large display currents put spikes on the supply, and poor power and ground routing can upset the chip or the controller. Keep supply and ground traces short and wide, especially when the chip and controller are on separate boards, and place at least a 0.1 µF monolithic or ceramic capacitor and an electrolytic of 100 µF or more across the supply close to the chip. In harsh environments the host can refresh the chip every few seconds, reloading the digit registers and turning the display back on.

The interface routines are largely compatible with the CH450's, whose subroutines and examples can be used directly. For four-digit display, the 18-pin CH455K is broadly pin-compatible with the 20-pin CH450K, using only DIG4 to DIG7 of the CH450K, with the 18-pin package aligned to the right-hand end of the 20-pin one.
Ways of driving large, high-voltage or high-current digits follow the CH452 datasheet.
